title: Machiavelli
orientation: Russell presents Machiavelli as the Renaissance's one figure of supreme eminence in political philosophy: a scientific, empirical analyst of how power is actually won, held, and lost, who is conventionally vilified mainly because he frankly describes political conduct that most other theorists disguise with pious language. The chapter reconstructs both the notorious 'immoral' doctrine of The Prince and the more republican, liberal doctrine of the Discourses, arguing the two are complementary rather than contradictory once means and ends are properly distinguished.
historical_background: Machiavelli (1467-1527) was a Florentine who entered government service in 1498, immediately after Savonarola's execution, and served in it -- including on diplomatic missions -- until the Medici restoration of 1512, when he was arrested, acquitted, and retired to the countryside. The Prince (1513) was written and dedicated to Lorenzo the Magnificent's grandson in a failed bid to win Medici favor, while the longer, more republican Discourses (a commentary on Livy) was written around the same time. Machiavelli died in 1527, the same year as the sack of Rome, which Russell treats as also marking the death of the Italian Renaissance.
philosophical_problems: Can political theory be conducted as a value-neutral science of means to given ends, independent of whether those ends are good or bad?
Is the conventional moral condemnation of Machiavelli's realism about power itself a form of hypocrisy?
What is the true relationship between political skill (virtù) and political virtue, and can 'success' be studied scientifically apart from the goodness of what is pursued?
Is a community best understood as something a lawgiver can create all at once (as Lycurgus supposedly created Sparta), or as an organic growth that statesmen can only partially shape?

philosophers_discussed.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's sole primary subject: his life, The Prince, and the Discourses are examined in detail as the first genuinely modern, empirical treatment of politics, distinguishing questions of political ends from the separate, quasi-scientific question of effective means.

schools_discussed: Classical (Greek and Roman) republican political thought, as revived by Machiavelli

core_concepts.name: Machiavelli's separation of means from ends (the 'science of success')
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Machiavelli treats politics scientifically: he studies what actually works to gain and keep power, without moralizing about whether the goals pursued are good or bad. Russell argues this makes his method genuinely value-neutral, so that the same science of political success is equally useful to a 'saint' and a 'sinner,' since both must achieve their purposes to accomplish anything.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's reconstruction: 'His political philosophy is scientific and empirical, based upon his own experience of affairs, concerned to set forth the means to assigned ends, regardless of the question whether the ends are to be considered good or bad'; 'Success' means the achievement of your purpose, whatever it may be... the science, once established, will be just as useful to the saint as to the sinner.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is, for Russell, Machiavelli's central and most defensible innovation, distinguishing him sharply from moralizing political theorists before and after him.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed from Machiavelli's direct experience as a Florentine diplomat and observer of fifteenth-century Italian statecraft.
examples: The detailed analysis of Caesar Borgia's methods of conquest and consolidation of power
objections: The science of success is studied more easily in the successes of the wicked than of the good, since successful sinners are historically more numerous than successful saints
competing_positions: Medieval conceptions of 'legitimate' power derived from the Pope or Emperor, or from biblical grounds (e.g., events in the Garden of Eden), which Machiavelli entirely omits
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates later realist and empirical approaches to political theory, including, Russell suggests, applicability to twentieth-century power politics.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicitly severs political argument from Christian or biblical grounding.

core_concepts.name: The doctrine of The Prince: the ruler's necessary use of deception and force
core_concepts.plain_explanation: A ruler who is always good will be destroyed; he must combine the cunning of the fox with the ferocity of the lion, keeping faith only when it is advantageous, and above all appearing virtuous and religious even when he is not, since most people judge by appearances.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Machiavelli's explicit repudiation of received morality for rulers, illustrated in Chapter XVIII ('In What Way Princes Must Keep Faith'): rulers 'should keep faith when it pays to do so, but not otherwise,' must 'disguise this character well, and... be a great feigner and dissembler,' with Alexander VI cited approvingly as a supreme practitioner of successful deception.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is the doctrine responsible for Machiavelli's notorious reputation ('Machiavellian'), which Russell argues is misunderstood when read in isolation from the Discourses.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Drawn from the political conduct of fifteenth- and early sixteenth-century Italian rulers, especially Caesar Borgia and Pope Alexander VI.
examples: Caesar Borgia's conquest of the Romagna and manipulation of the College of Cardinals
Alexander VI's habitual deception, praised by Machiavelli for its skillful execution
objections: Conventional morality condemns deception and faithlessness as inherently wrong, regardless of political effectiveness
competing_positions: The more republican and liberal doctrine of the Discourses
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Gave rise to the term 'Machiavellian' and to a long tradition of realist political theory; Russell explicitly compares it to Hitler's Reichstag fire, 1934 purge, and post-Munich betrayal.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The chapter on ecclesiastical principalities notably conceals Machiavelli's franker views (expressed instead in the Discourses) out of deference to a newly elected Medici pope.

core_concepts.name: The republican doctrine of the Discourses: checks and balances and the value of liberty
core_concepts.plain_explanation: In his longer, more sincere work, Machiavelli argues for constitutions that balance the power of prince, nobles, and people against each other, praises Sparta's constitution (as more balanced than Athens's), values the Roman republic's conflict of Senate and people, and argues -- against most classical authors -- that the common people are generally wiser and more constant than princes.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's account of the Discourses' 'doctrine of checks and balances... set forth explicitly': 'Princes, nobles, and people should all have a part in the Constitution... then these three powers will keep each other reciprocally in check,' with a stated preference for popular government grounded not in natural rights but in the empirical observation that popular governments are 'less cruel, unscrupulous, and inconstant than tyrannies.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as at least as important as the more famous 'immoral' doctrines of The Prince, and as a direct historical channel through which classical republican political thought (largely dormant since antiquity) was transmitted to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Modeled on Livy's history of the Roman Republic and on the constitutions of Sparta (Lycurgus) and Athens (Solon).
examples: Praise of the Spartan constitution of Lycurgus as more balanced than Solon's more democratic Athenian constitution
Praise of the Roman republican constitution's built-in conflict between Senate and people
competing_positions: Livy's and most other classical writers' view that princes are wiser and more constant than the people, which Machiavelli explicitly rejects
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes its resemblance to Montesquieu and its readability by 'an eighteenth-century liberal,' directly linking Machiavelli to the later theory of separation of powers.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Machiavelli treats religion instrumentally, as valuable for its social-cementing effect (citing Roman use of auguries) rather than for its truth.

core_concepts.name: Politics as fundamentally a question of power, not of abstract right
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Slogans like 'right will prevail' obscure the fact that whichever side wins does so because it commands superior power; though appearing virtuous can itself be a source of power (since it wins public support), this is a contingent, propagandistic advantage rather than proof that virtue always triumphs.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's synthesis of Machiavelli's implicit view: 'The question is ultimately one of power. To achieve a political end, power, of one kind or another, is necessary... it is an advantage in propaganda to seem more virtuous than your adversary, and that one way of seeming virtuous is to be virtuous,' but this is qualified by the observation that those already in power can control propaganda to appear virtuous regardless of their actual conduct.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Provides Russell's bridge between the 'immoral' and 'moral' halves of Machiavelli's doctrine, and generalizes it into a broader claim about the historical role of virtue as a (contingent) instrument of political success.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Illustrated by the growing power of the Church in the eleventh-thirteenth centuries and the success of the Reformation in the sixteenth, both attributed partly to a public perception of comparative virtue.
examples: No one could mention Alexander VI's sins in a New York or Boston public school, illustrating how those in power control propaganda about their own virtue
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: connects the appearance of virtue to religious and political legitimacy.

arguments.title: Russell's synthesis of the 'moral' and 'immoral' Machiavelli
premises: There are certain political goods -- national independence, security, and a well-ordered (balanced) constitution -- that are ends worth pursuing.
Pursuing any political end requires effective means, and the question of effective means can be studied scientifically, independent of whether the end is good or bad.

Since successful sinners historically outnumber successful saints, the science of political success is, in practice, more easily illustrated by unscrupulous examples -- but it is equally available and useful to anyone pursuing any end, including a good one.
arguments.conclusion: Machiavelli's 'immoral' doctrine of effective means (The Prince) and his 'moral' doctrine of good constitutional ends (the Discourses) are not contradictory but complementary: he is a scientist of political means who happens, when he expresses his own preferences, to favor good ends.
arguments.explanation: Russell explicitly states he is constructing 'a synthesis (which Machiavelli himself did not make)' of the two halves of the doctrine, attributing the constructive move to his own reading rather than to an explicit statement by Machiavelli.
objections: It is not always true that the more virtuous side wins, since those in power can control propaganda to make themselves appear virtuous regardless of conduct
In chaotic periods (like Machiavelli's own), 'obvious knavery frequently succeeds,' producing cynicism that forgives anything that pays
implications: Suggests that the wisest political conduct depends on the moral character of the population one operates among: politicians behave better when dependent on a virtuous, well-informed public than on an indifferent or censored one.

arguments.title: Machiavelli's case for Caesar Borgia as a model 'to be imitated'
premises: Caesar Borgia faced a genuinely difficult political problem: becoming his father Alexander VI's sole dynastic heir, conquering territory in the Pope's name that would become his own after Alexander's death, and securing a friendly successor pope.
Borgia pursued this problem with exceptional skill, and failed only through the 'extraordinary malignity of fortune' -- falling gravely ill at the exact moment of his father's death.
Machiavelli, intimately acquainted with Borgia's methods, states he finds 'nothing to blame' in reviewing all of Borgia's actions.
arguments.conclusion: Borgia should be 'held as an example to be imitated by all who by fortune and with the arms of others have risen to power.'
arguments.explanation: Russell notes this praise is for Borgia's skill and dexterity, not for his (bad) purposes; Machiavelli separately, in the Discourses, criticizes the Borgia-Alexander VI papacy for keeping Italy divided, showing that admiration of political virtù and patriotic judgment of ends coexisted in Machiavelli's mind without being synthesized by him.
objections: The wickedness of Borgia's and Alexander VI's methods 'soon became legendary,' and it is difficult to disentangle truth from later exaggeration
implications: Illustrates the Renaissance's 'quasi-artistic admiration of dexterity,' which Russell says was much greater in Machiavelli's Italy than in earlier or later centuries.

key_distinctions: Means (a value-neutral science of effective political action) vs. ends (a separate question of which political goals are good)
The Prince's realistic, ends-omitting counsel to an actual (Medici) prince vs. the Discourses' more sincere, republican commentary on Livy
Admiration of political skill/dexterity vs. approval of the purposes that skill serves
A community created all at once by a lawgiver (Lycurgus, Solon) vs. a community as an organic, gradually evolving growth
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell connects Machiavelli's revival of classical republican political thought (checks and balances, the value of 'liberty') directly to the political theory of republican Greece and Rome, noting that this dimension of ancient thought had lain dormant -- ignored by Neoplatonists, Arabs, and Schoolmen who cared about Plato's and Aristotle's metaphysics but not their politics -- until the rise of Italian city-states made it newly relevant.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell explicitly traces Machiavelli's doctrine of checks and balances forward to Montesquieu and eighteenth-century liberalism, and contrasts Machiavelli's power-based, non-biblical account of legitimacy with later writers, even as late as Locke, who still tried to derive political conclusions from what happened in the Garden of Eden. The chapter also anticipates Hobbes (Chapter VIII), whose theory of the State Russell will describe as even more modern than Machiavelli's.
political_social_context: The chapter is inseparable from the political chaos of fifteenth-century Italy -- illegitimate rulers, corrupt papal elections, the career of Caesar Borgia, and Machiavelli's own diplomatic career and downfall with the 1512 Medici restoration -- and closes with Russell's contemporary application of Machiavellian analysis to twentieth-century totalitarian politics (Hitler's Reichstag fire, 1934 purge, and post-Munich betrayal; the 'mythical Lycurgus' compared to modern 'terrifying' lawgivers in Russia and Germany).
religion_science_culture_context: Machiavelli's treatment of religion is presented as purely instrumental: he values religion (as the Romans used augury) for its function as social cement, not for its truth, and criticizes the contemporary Church both for undermining religious belief through its own bad conduct and for its temporal power's role in keeping Italy politically divided.
russell_presentation: Russell defends Machiavelli against what he considers largely hypocritical moral outrage, arguing that 'much of the conventional obloquy that attaches to his name is due to the indignation of hypocrites who hate the frank avowal of evil-doing,' while still conceding that 'a good deal... genuinely demands criticism.' He characterizes Machiavelli's political philosophy as 'scientific and empirical,' concerned with means rather than ends, and constructs his own explicit synthesis of the 'immoral' Prince and the more republican, liberal Discourses, arguing readers who skip the latter get 'a very one-sided view of his doctrine.' Russell is notably contemporary and pointed in his evaluation, suggesting 'our age... can better appreciate Machiavelli' because 'some of the most notable successes of our time have been achieved by methods as base as any employed in Renaissance Italy,' explicitly citing Hitler's Reichstag fire, 1934 purge, and betrayal after Munich as actions Machiavelli 'would have applauded... as an artistic connoisseur in statecraft.' He also identifies a genuine limitation in Machiavelli's thought: an outdated, ancient-style conception of political communities as things a lawgiver can create outright (like the mythical Lycurgus), rather than as organic growths -- a conception Russell says has been undermined by evolutionary theory, yet has become disturbingly relevant again given the deliberate, 'mechanistic' creation of new societies in Russia and Germany in his own time.
critical_context: Common scholarly debate: Russell's interpretive move of treating The Prince and the Discourses as expressing a single, coherent underlying position (means-focused science of politics serving good ends) is itself one major interpretive tradition among several; other readings treat the apparent tension between the two works as reflecting genuine ambivalence, irony, or evolution in Machiavelli's thought (or as reflecting the different genres and audiences of each work) rather than a synthesis Machiavelli himself implicitly held but never stated -- a point Russell himself flags by noting explicitly that this is 'a synthesis... which Machiavelli himself did not make.'
key_takeaways: Russell defends Machiavelli's realism as largely misunderstood: his 'shocking' reputation partly reflects hypocrisy on the part of critics unwilling to admit political conduct they themselves tolerate.

The Prince treats politics as a value-neutral science of effective means, separate from the question of whether the ends pursued are good; a ruler must combine the fox's cunning with the lion's ferocity and, above all, appear virtuous.

The Discourses present a much more republican, liberal Machiavelli, advocating checks and balances among prince, nobles, and people, and preferring popular government on empirical (not rights-based) grounds.

Russell constructs his own synthesis of these two works: Machiavelli's science of means can serve good ends just as well as bad ones, even though Machiavelli himself never states this synthesis explicitly.
Machiavelli revives classical republican political thought (checks and balances, the value of liberty) dormant since antiquity, directly influencing eighteenth-century figures like Montesquieu.

Russell finds Machiavelli's thought newly and disturbingly relevant to his own time, comparing his admiration of political dexterity to Hitler's methods and his account of lawgivers creating societies wholesale to the deliberate 'mechanistic' creation of new political orders in Russia and Germany.
study_notes:
The single most useful move for understanding this chapter is Russell's means/ends distinction: Machiavelli is not (on Russell's reading) recommending evil ends, but describing, scientifically and without moralizing, what means actually work to gain and hold power -- a description that is, in principle, just as usable by a benevolent ruler as by a tyrant. Keep the two texts distinct as you read: The Prince, written to flatter and advise an actual Medici ruler, foregrounds the 'immoral' doctrine of deception and force; the Discourses, a commentary on Livy written for Machiavelli himself rather than a patron, foregrounds the 'moral,' republican doctrine of checks and balances and a preference for popular government. Russell's own synthesis (means are separable from, and serve, whatever ends one holds) is his interpretive contribution, not a claim that Machiavelli stated this integration explicitly.

Notice also how directly Russell brings this fifteenth/sixteenth-century material into conversation with his own mid-twentieth-century present: the comparisons to Hitler and to the 'mechanistic' creation of new societies in Russia and Germany are not incidental color but central to his argument that Machiavelli's supposedly outdated, 'ancient' conception of political communities as things a lawgiver can simply create has become, in the era of totalitarian social engineering, more relevant rather than less.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Not moral 'virtue' in the ordinary sense, but skill, boldness, and effectiveness in gaining and using political power.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Though Russell does not use the Italian term directly, the quality he describes -- admired skill and dexterity in political action, exemplified by Caesar Borgia, judged independently of the moral worth of the ends pursued -- corresponds to what is commonly called Machiavellian virtù in later scholarship.
related_concepts: The doctrine of The Prince: the ruler's necessary use of deception and force

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A system of government in which different groups (e.g., a prince, nobles, and the people) share power and limit each other, preventing any one from dominating.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The constitutional principle, set forth explicitly in Machiavelli's Discourses, that apportioning power among prince, nobles, and people so that each checks the others produces greater political stability -- a principle Russell traces forward to Montesquieu and eighteenth-century liberal constitutionalism.
related_concepts: The republican doctrine of the Discourses: checks and balances and the value of liberty

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Machiavelli's idea that studying what actually makes political action succeed can be done objectively, the same way one might study any other practical skill, without judging whether the goal itself is good.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's characterization of Machiavelli's core methodological innovation: the study of effective political means as a value-neutral science, applicable equally to good and bad ends, distinguished from the separate question of the goodness of the ends pursued.
related_concepts: Machiavelli's separation of means from ends (the 'science of success')

questions.prompt: According to Russell, why is much of the conventional condemnation of Machiavelli unfair?
questions.answer: Because much of the outrage against Machiavelli comes from hypocrites who are shocked less by the political conduct he describes than by his frank willingness to describe it openly; many other political actors would seem equally shocking if they were equally free from humbug.
questions.explanation: Russell still concedes some of the criticism of Machiavelli is genuinely deserved, treating him as an expression of the moral character of his age.

questions.prompt: What is Machiavelli's central methodological innovation, according to Russell, and why does he consider it valuable?
questions.answer: Treating political theory as a scientific, empirical study of the means to a given end, independent of whether that end is good or bad -- a 'science of success' that Russell argues would be just as useful to a saint pursuing a good end as to a sinner pursuing a bad one.
questions.explanation: This separation of means from ends is what makes Machiavelli's approach, in Russell's view, genuinely modern.

questions.prompt: Contrast the political doctrine of The Prince with that of the Discourses.
questions.answer: The Prince, dedicated to a Medici ruler, presents the notorious 'immoral' doctrine that a prince must be willing to deceive, break faith when advantageous, and merely appear virtuous. The Discourses, a more sincere commentary on Livy, sets forth a republican doctrine of checks and balances among prince, nobles, and people, praises the Spartan and Roman constitutions, and argues (against most classical authors) that the people are generally wiser and more constant than princes.
questions.explanation: Russell argues that reading only The Prince gives 'a very one-sided view' of Machiavelli's overall doctrine.

questions.prompt: Why does Machiavelli praise Caesar Borgia, and what limitation does Russell note in this praise?
questions.answer: Machiavelli praises Borgia's exceptional skill in pursuing a difficult political problem (securing his father's dynastic ambitions, conquering territory in the Pope's name, and manipulating the College of Cardinals), even calling him a model to be imitated. Russell notes this praise is purely for Borgia's dexterity, not his purposes, since Machiavelli elsewhere (in the Discourses) criticizes the Borgia-Alexander VI papacy for keeping Italy divided.
questions.explanation: This shows love of skill and patriotic concern for Italian unity coexisting, unsynthesized, in Machiavelli's mind.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's own synthesis of the 'moral' and 'immoral' parts of Machiavelli's doctrine.
questions.answer: Premise: there are political goods worth pursuing -- national independence, security, and a well-ordered, balanced constitution. Premise: achieving any political end requires effective means, and the question of effective means can be studied scientifically, apart from whether the end is good. Premise: since successful sinners are more numerous historically than successful saints, examples of the 'science of success' are more often drawn from unscrupulous cases, but the science itself is equally useful to good and bad actors alike. Conclusion: Machiavelli's realistic account of political means (The Prince) and his preference for good, balanced political ends (the Discourses) are complementary rather than contradictory, once means and ends are properly separated.
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly notes that Machiavelli himself never stated this synthesis; it is Russell's own interpretive reconstruction.

questions.prompt: Which fifteenth-century Florentine political theorist is credited by Russell as the Renaissance's only figure of supreme eminence in political philosophy?
questions.explanation: Russell opens the chapter by stating that although the Renaissance produced no important theoretical philosopher, it produced this one figure of supreme eminence specifically in political philosophy.
